name: PT Calculus Global Ventures Tbk

frontmatter.title: A deposit book wearing an asset manager's story
frontmatter.summary: Calculus Global Ventures is a listed investment book, not a scaled asset manager: almost all of its assets are time deposits, promissory notes and fund units earning a low single-digit return, the fund management subsidiary's fees only just cover its own costs, and no dividend has been paid in two years. The shares trade far above book on a change-of-control story. We initiate at SELL.
thesis: The balance sheet is the business. Equity of IDR553.7bn is almost entirely deposits, notes and fund units, and that book earned 4.5% in the last audited year and earns 3.9% on our forecast [S3][S4].
Fees do not pay their way. Nine months of revenue of IDR7.2bn against operating costs of IDR7.1bn leaves the profit line to interest of IDR9.4bn and other income of IDR16.1bn [S4].
The book yields less than the risk-free rate because it sits in small-bank deposits and one offshore promissory note, and the company discloses no assets under management for its fund arm [S3].
Control changed at Rp88 a share in November 2025; the shares reached Rp790 and still trade at Rp264, which is 2.3x book [S5][S6].
We value the book at 0.2x book and target Rp18, -93.1%. The price implies a sustainable ROE of 24.5%, far above anything this portfolio has delivered [S3].

catalysts.event: Rollover or repayment terms of the Summit International promissory notes that carry most of the interest income; the September 2026 balance sheet shows the book already rolled once without disclosure
FY2026 audited accounts, the first full year under the new controller and the first evidence of how the investment book is being run
FY2026 annual report: whether assets under management, client numbers or a deployment plan are finally disclosed
Annual general meeting: any resolution on a first dividend out of the accumulated book

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Calculus Global Ventures Tbk with a **SELL** rating and a target of Rp18, against a last price of Rp264. That is an expected return of -93.1%. The target is built from the assets the company owns rather than from the story attached to them: the fundamental value per share is Rp18, rolled forward one year at the cost of equity to Rp20, probability-weighted at Rp23 across our scenarios, and then cut by a 20.0% liquidity and governance discount to reach the target. Every scenario carries a positive value - the bear case is an earnings stress worth Rp7, not a write-down - and the discount after the weighting prices liquidity alone, so the same risk is not deducted twice. A principal loss on the concentrated deposit or the promissory notes is disclosed as a risk in the scenario section and is not in any scenario number; it would take the value below every figure in this report, which is why the call does not depend on it.

What the company owns is a portfolio, not a franchise. Group equity of IDR553.7bn is held almost entirely as cash of IDR32.1bn, short-term investments of IDR501.0bn and a securities portfolio of IDR18.6bn, and the short-term investments are in turn time deposits recorded at IDR493.0bn at the last year end plus promissory notes [S4]. The operating subsidiary, PT Foster Asset Management, is a licensed investment manager with two mutual funds and a discretionary mandate book, and it charges fees of IDR7.2bn over the first nine months of the year while the group spends IDR7.1bn to run itself [S4]. On the same accounts, profit of IDR15.7bn came from deposit interest of IDR9.4bn and other income of IDR16.1bn, not from the fee business [S4].

The shares did not get here on earnings. A 32.2% block held through PT Kencana Selaras Sejahtera changed hands to Calculus Investment Pte Ltd in November 2025 at Rp88 a share, the stock rose by more than three times in a month, and the exchange suspended trading for a day in the middle of the run [S5][S6]. A mandatory tender offer for up to 67.8% of the capital followed and completed in February 2026 without changing control [S2]. The market now pays 2.3x book for a book that returns 3.9%.

Our variant view is deliberately unromantic. A change of control can create value here, but only through one of three routes, and none has been evidenced yet: redeploying the portfolio into assets that earn more than a deposit, scaling the fund manager until its fees cover group costs with something left over, or paying out the book. The company has disclosed no assets under management, no client numbers, no deployment plan and no dividend policy [S2][S4]. Without one of those, the value of the equity is the value of the deposits and notes it holds, and the return on those assets supports 0.2x book, not the 2.3x book the market pays.

The two things that move our target are the return on the book and the rate we discount it at. Every extra point of sustainable ROE is worth multiples of the current target, which is why this is a call on capital allocation rather than on the fund industry. We carry the third leg as a 20.0% liquidity and governance discount for a counter that has been suspended once in the year, has an offshore controlling shareholder with a single named beneficial owner, and trades far below a normal free-float turnover.

Small listed investment vehicles are common in emerging markets and their economics are simple: the
share price can drift far from the value of the underlying portfolio for long periods because few
investors do the arithmetic on the portfolio, and because the controlling shareholder's intentions are
the real driver of value. Where a vehicle is bought for its listing rather than its assets, the new
owner usually injects a business into it. Until that happens, the asset value is the anchor, and the
discount or premium to it reflects expectations about the injection rather than current cash flows.

PT Calculus Global Ventures Tbk is a listed investment entity. It was formerly PT Buana Artha Anugerah Tbk, and it took its present name after an extraordinary general meeting in February 2026 that also amended Article 3 of its articles of association on purposes, objectives and business activities, and replaced the board [S2]. The FY2025 annual report is published under the new name and describes the company as an investment entity with a long-term orientation, which is the most accurate description of what the accounts show [S2]. Consolidated operations run through subsidiaries, of which the operating one is PT Foster Asset Management, a licensed investment manager [S2].

The product set is small and conventional. Through Foster Asset Management the group manages a Foster Equity Fund, a Foster Fixed Income Fund and discretionary portfolio mandates, with the equity fund constituted as a collective investment contract under the capital markets law and custodied at a domestic bank [S2]. The funds are distributed to retail investors and the discretionary mandates are written for institutional and high-net-worth clients, which is the standard shape of a second-tier Indonesian manager. The company has not launched a green or sharia product, although the annual report says a green-themed fund is being prepared [S2].

Revenue is one line: investment manager service fees. The audited revenue note for FY2025 shows fees of IDR6.6bn, against IDR4.1bn a year earlier, with no other revenue category disclosed [S3]. The management commentary puts the same number in its own words and reports total segment profit of IDR23.3bn, up from IDR19.1bn, of which the investment manager segment contributed 57.3% [S2]. Read together, those two disclosures say that the fee business is the largest profit contributor inside a group whose reported net profit is dominated by interest and mark-to-market income, because the segment measure is struck before those items and before unallocated costs.

The cost base is a single operating expense pool. Total operating expenses were IDR8.0bn in FY2025, and IDR7.1bn in the first nine months of FY2026 against revenue of IDR7.2bn [S3][S4]. That is the central fact of the business model: the fee business does not pay for itself. On the audited FY2025 comparison the fee line of IDR6.6bn against operating expenses of IDR8.0bn is a loss from operations of IDR-1.4bn, a negative operating margin of more than a fifth [S2]. The manager is therefore not close to break-even, let alone self-funding, and every rupiah of reported profit comes from the investment portfolio rather than from managing money. Employee numbers are small at 17, consistent with a manager that outsources custody, distribution infrastructure and back office, and there is no branch network or geographic footprint to speak of beyond Jakarta [S0][S2].

Strategy under the new controller is stated at the level of intention rather than plan. The corporate secretary said at the time of the tender offer that the company remained focused on existing programmes, strategy and business development, and the annual report repeats the vision and mission as still relevant [S2][S6]. Nothing in the filings sets out a target for assets under management, a fee or cost target, a capital deployment programme, or a dividend policy. The purposes clause was widened, which gives the company room to enter new lines of business without another shareholder vote, and that optionality is real but unpriced in our numbers because there is no disclosed transaction to price [S2].

Competitively the group is a challenger with no scale advantage. It competes for retail subscriptions against bank-owned managers with captive distribution and against independent managers with longer track records, and for discretionary mandates against everyone. Its assets are its licence, its two funds and the investment book that gives it a balance sheet to seed new products. The controlling shareholder is Calculus Investment Pte Ltd, a Singapore company owned by Calculus Ventures Pte Ltd, whose ultimate beneficial owner the company's disclosure names as David Darius H.K.; the seller of the block was PT Kencana Selaras Sejahtera, which is almost wholly owned by Ronny Lukito [S6]. Insider holdings are 32.2% of the capital and the free float is 67.8% [S0].

The Indonesian mutual fund industry ended 2025 with assets under management of Rp996.0 trillion, having grown by roughly a quarter over the year, and with 20.32 million single investor identification accounts on the register [S2]. Growth of that order in a market where retail participation is still rising is the reason a small manager can grow fees quickly: Foster's own revenue rose from IDR4.1bn to IDR6.6bn in one year and by more than half again in the first nine months of FY2026 [S3][S4]. The industry is large relative to this company, which is both the opportunity and the problem, because a manager with no disclosed assets under management cannot be shown to hold any meaningful share of it.

The demand drivers are familiar and mostly cyclical. Household savings flow into funds when deposit rates are unexciting and equity returns are positive, and they stop flowing when markets fall, so flows follow performance with a lag. Regulation is a second driver: the licensing and conduct regime administered by the financial services authority sets capital, custody and reporting requirements, and the annual report itself is prepared under the rules for public company annual reports and sustainable finance [S2]. Compulsory disclosure of fees and portfolio holdings pushes the industry toward transparency and compresses the margins available on plain vanilla products, which favours managers that can differentiate on distribution or performance rather than on price.

The competitive structure is unfavourable to sub-scale independents, and the company's own annual report names competition with similar companies as a principal business risk, met by product differentiation and marketing rather than by scale or price [S2]. Fixed costs of compliance, systems and custody are largely invariant to assets, so unit economics improve sharply with size, and the largest managers are owned by banks and insurers that can place products through their own branches. Five forces read: supplier power is low because custody and administration are commoditised; buyer power is high because retail investors switch funds on a few quarters of relative performance and institutional mandates are tendered; the threat of new entrants is moderate because the licence is not hard to obtain but distribution is; substitutes are strong, with deposits, government bonds and direct equity all competing for the same savings; and rivalry is intense and increasingly price-based. The group's moat, on that reading, is thin: a licence, two small funds and a balance sheet [S2].

The industry's economics also explain why this company's profit does not look like a manager's. A manager earns a percentage of assets under management, so its revenue is a function of a number the company does not disclose, and its costs are mostly people and regulation. When fees and costs sit at the same level, as they do here, the equity story reduces to what else the balance sheet holds [S4]. Our macro context matters for that balance sheet in two ways: the rupiah path we carry in the house deck influences imported inflation and therefore the policy rate, and the policy rate sets what a deposit book can earn. With the risk-free rate at 7.4% and our cost of equity at 11.9%, a portfolio of deposits and notes earning a few percent cannot produce a return that justifies a premium to book unless the assets change [S3].

Asset management is a capital-light, operating-leverage business: revenue scales with assets while
compliance, technology and custody costs scale with regulation, not with size. That is why the industry
consolidates and why small managers either specialise in a niche, get bought by a distributor, or slowly
lose share. A manager owned by a listed vehicle with a large cash pile is unusual, and the usual outcome
is that the cash is either deployed into the manager's own products to seed them, distributed to
shareholders, or used to buy another manager.

Revenue has grown quickly from a small base. Investment manager fees were IDR4.1bn in FY2024 and IDR6.6bn in FY2025, and the first nine months of FY2026 already show IDR7.2bn [S3][S4]. Our FY2026E revenue of IDR9.6bn assumes the nine-month run-rate holds through the fourth quarter and then decelerates; the growth path is in the model but it is close to cosmetic, because fees are the smaller half of the profit equation. What matters is the interest line, and that is a function of the size of the portfolio and the rates the company negotiates with its banks.

Those rates are the weakest number in the model, and we state the arithmetic rather than assume it away, on a consistent period basis. The audited year is the anchor: deposit interest of IDR8.5bn on a time-deposit book of IDR378.0bn is a yield of a little over two per cent for FY2025 [S3]. The nine-month figure is unaudited and has to be annualised before it is compared with a full year, not set beside it: nine-month 2026 deposit interest of IDR9.4bn, annualised, is a yield of roughly three and a third per cent on a deposit book of the same order as the IDR378.0bn held at the year end - a clear step up on the audited year rather than a marginal one [S4]. That repricing is the one piece of evidence that the book is being run closer to market, and we use it in the bull case rather than in the base.

The comparison also carries an inconsistency we cannot resolve from outside the company, and we would rather name it than smooth it. The 9M2026 filing's own comparative column shows nine-month 2025 deposit interest of IDR11.4bn, which is larger than the IDR8.5bn the audited FY2025 accounts show for the entire year [S3][S4]. Both cannot describe the same twelve months; the audited figure governs the history, and the candidates are a fourth-quarter 2025 reversal, a reclassification between the unaudited comparative and the audited year, or a restatement we have not seen. We cannot test which, so we treat the audited number as the calibration point, treat the 9M2026 annualised yield as indicative of where the book now earns, and cap the bull's normalisation at the yield the nine-month accounts already print rather than at a market rate. We do not put the higher yield in the base case because one unaudited nine-month period does not outweigh two audited years, and that is the disciplined version of the most-likely test: the base re-runs last year's economics, and the drift above it is sourced in the bull.

Reported profit is volatile in a way that revenue is not. Net profit attributable to owners was IDR4.2bn in FY2024 and IDR22.9bn in FY2025, a jump driven by a fair-value gain of IDR9.8bn on listed shares rather than by fees [S3]. The nine months to September 2026 produced IDR15.7bn, of which deposit interest was IDR9.4bn and other income IDR16.1bn [S4]. On our assumptions, FY2026E net profit is IDR21.0bn, or Rp4 per share on 4,800.0m shares, giving an ROE of 3.9% on opening equity and a book value per share of Rp116 at the year end [S4]. The reduction against FY2025 reflects the absence of a repeat of the mark-to-market gain, not a deterioration in the underlying portfolio.

The portfolio itself is short-dated and heavily concentrated. At the last year end, short-term investments stood at IDR493.0bn, of which time deposits were IDR378.0bn and promissory notes IDR115.0bn; by September 2026 the total had risen to IDR501.0bn with cash of IDR32.1bn and a securities portfolio of IDR18.6bn alongside [S3][S4]. One bank holds a deposit of IDR322.0bn, which is the bulk of the deposit book, and the promissory notes are issued by a single offshore counterparty [S3]. That concentration was re-arranged wholesale during FY2025: the identical IDR322.0bn that sat at Bank Hibank Indonesia (formerly Bank Mayora) at the end of FY2024 was not there at the end of FY2025, and the IDR322.0bn at Bank Ina Perdana was not there a year earlier [S3]. The deposit was moved between two small banks in one year and the filings give no reason. We checked the related-party channel because that is the obvious explanation for such a switch: the notes state that all cash in banks is placed with third parties and that there are no placements with related parties, and no revenue from related parties is disclosed [S3]. We accept that disclosure and still flag the migration as unexplained - a complete turnover of the largest asset with no disclosed economic gain is a governance question even where it is not a related-party one, and it is quantified above as a share of the book. Interest earned on deposits was IDR8.5bn in FY2025 and IDR8.0bn on the notes, so the notes, at roughly a third of the deposits in size, produced a similar amount of income: the note coupon is materially above deposit rates, which is the compensation for counterparty and liquidity risk on a name the company does not rate or describe in detail [S3].

Cost control is adequate in absolute terms and poor in relative terms. Operating expenses of IDR8.0bn in FY2025 were actually below the prior year, and the nine-month figure of IDR7.1bn is close to the full-year level, so the run-rate is stable [S3][S4]. But against fee revenue of IDR7.2bn for the same nine months, the operating margin on the fee business is approximately zero before any allocation of group overhead. Investors in an asset manager normally pay for that margin; here the fee business is a cost centre that happens to hold the licence, and the value comes from the capital behind it.

The balance sheet is unusual and simple. Equity attributable to owners is IDR553.7bn, total assets are close behind it, and there are no bank borrowings: liabilities are payables and accruals, so the company is unlevered at the group level [S4]. Capital expenditure is negligible because there are no fixed assets of consequence, and working capital is not a meaningful line for a manager that collects fees monthly. Capital allocation, by contrast, is a real decision: payout has been zero, the company states that it did not distribute a dividend in the last two years and allocated all profit to capital, and we carry a zero payout through the forecast [S2][S4]. With a zero payout and a positive return on equity, the book compounds, which is why our equity line rises from IDR538.0bn to IDR651.4bn by FY2030E at an ROE held flat at 3.9%.

Earnings quality is the weakest part of the story, and we flag it before the valuation. First, profit is not cash: the FY2025 result includes IDR9.8bn of unrealised fair-value gains, and the reported return on equity therefore overstates what the portfolio can distribute [S3]. The split is starker than that. The audited comparison shows a loss from operations of IDR-1.4bn and other income of IDR24.7bn, so the whole pre-tax profit of the year is other income and the operation is a negative contributor [S2]; the fair-value gain is under half of that other-income line, so describing the result as a mark-to-market year understates how much of it is coupon and fee-like income on the portfolio and overstates the recurring franchise. Recurring for our purposes is deposit and note interest plus the fee line less all operating costs; non-recurring is the fair-value gain and any one-off on the securities book. On that definition the recurring base is thin and the return we forecast is interest on a short-dated book, not a franchise. Second, the audited and unaudited numbers do not tie: the nine-month 2025 statement shows deposit interest of IDR11.4bn, while the audited full year shows IDR8.5bn for deposits, which implies either a large reclassification between interest and other income in the fourth quarter or a restatement of the comparative, and either way investors should weight the audited figures and expect fourth-quarter true-ups [S3][S4]. Third, the counterparty profile is unverified: a deposit concentrated at a single small bank and a promissory note issued by an offshore company are the two places where the book could lose principal, and the filings give no credit assessment of either [S3]. Fourth, there is no assets under management disclosure, so the fee revenue cannot be decomposed into assets and fee rate, and we cannot tell whether the growth came from subscriptions, performance or a fee change [S2][S4]. Finally, a zero dividend means the cash generation of the group is never tested by a distribution, which is how a listed vehicle with a large securities portfolio can carry marks that are never realised.

We restate rather than smooth. Where the data pack's capital-market history disagreed with the filings we took the filing: revenue, net profit, equity, total assets, shares outstanding and interest income in this model come from the audited FY2025 statements and the September 2026 quarterly report, keyed as facts and applied by the engine [S3][S4]. The forecast is then a short, deliberately unheroic extension: fees grow, costs grow with them, the portfolio earns what the last actual earned, the payout stays at zero and the book compounds at 3.9% in perpetuity with terminal growth of 2.0% [S3]. We should be explicit about that growth rate rather than let it look like a haircut: with zero payout the book grows at the return it earns, so the intrinsic growth rate of this company is its ROE, not two per cent. Setting terminal growth below the ROE is the generous choice for the valuation, because the Gordon multiple (ROE less g) over (COE less g) falls as g rises when the ROE is below the cost of equity - the gap between the two widens as the denominator shrinks. Two per cent is therefore the friendliest defensible number, not a conservatism, and a growth rate equal to the ROE would take the warranted multiple toward zero.

The method set follows the industry card for financial holding companies. Justified price to book is the primary method because the company's value is its book and the return that book earns, not a multiple of a fee stream that barely covers its own costs. Residual income is the cross-check because it reads the same economics from the other side, charging the cost of equity against the book as it compounds, and it is the only method that values the retained cash explicitly rather than through a terminal multiple. Dividend discount is dropped because a zero payout makes it degenerate, and peer price to book is dropped because the cohort median is set by operating holding companies whose multiples describe businesses this company does not own. The P/E leg is dropped to zero. It was previously two fifths of the blend on a peer median attributed to the data pack; that multiple is not reproducible from the FINANCIAL_HOLDCOS cohort, whose trailing P/Es run from single digits to four figures with the median set by shells earning a negligible return on equity, and a multiple we cannot rebuild from named companies does not belong in a target. The weights are 70.0% to justified P/B and 30.0% to residual income, which is where the weight the DDM could not use now sits: with the earnings multiple withdrawn, the freed weight goes to the method family the industry card calls primary, not to a multiple of a fee stream.

The two methods agree on direction and differ on level: residual income values the shares at Rp8, -66.0% against the Rp22 of justified P/B. The gap is the terminal assumption. Justified P/B applies one Gordon multiple to a return that is flat forever; residual income charges the full cost of equity against a book that compounds at the return instead, so on a return below the cost of capital it is the harsher of the two by construction. We keep both weights rather than pick the flattering one, and the target therefore sits between them.

The cost of equity sets the answer, so it is worth being explicit line by line. The build is the risk-free rate of 7.4% minus the IDR default spread of 1.6% that the house deck applies to an Indonesian issuer, plus the product of the levered beta and the equity risk premium of 4.2% plus the country risk premium of 2.5%; company specific premia are 0.0%. The levered beta is 0.90: we do not override the FINANCIAL_HOLDCOS industry default of 0.90, because the house beta table carries no regression for this industry and a regression run on this stock would be contaminated by the control trade that tripled the price in a month, an event uncorrelated with the index [S5][S6]. The result is a cost of equity of 11.9% and, with no net debt, a WACC of 11.9%. Those two numbers are model outputs from the house rate inputs and the FINANCIAL_HOLDCOS beta default, not figures taken from a company filing, and no filing could supply them; the only source cited for this paragraph is the control trade that contaminates a regression [S5]. That is the low end of what the FINANCIAL_HOLDCOS cohort carries and below the operating holdcos, because the asset side is almost entirely time deposits, promissory notes and fund units [S4]; it is not below the risk-free rate, which is the test that matters, and an earlier build on an asserted beta of a fifth failed it. Removing that build and the non-reproducible earnings multiple accounts for the whole change in the target since the first draft.

One line of the build deserves an explanation because it looks backwards on a first read. We deduct the IDR default spread from the government yield before adding beta times the mature-market equity risk premium. That is deliberate and not a sign error: an Indonesian government yield already contains the sovereign default premium, so the quantity that belongs in a build which adds the country risk premium separately is the yield net of it, otherwise the country's credit risk is charged twice. The two operations are the same if the default spread and the country premium are equal, which is why the result is robust to the choice and why the cost of equity lands at the low end of the cohort rather than at the top.

The primary method produces a value of Rp22 per share, from a justified multiple of 0.2x book. That multiple is the ratio of the return the book earns over the growth we assume, divided by the cost of equity over the same growth: with a sustainable ROE of 3.9%, terminal growth of 2.0% and a cost of equity of 11.9%, a book that returns less than its cost of capital is worth less than book, and the arithmetic is unforgiving because the gap is large relative to the growth rate.

What the company owns is worth more than the earnings it produces, and the report should say the number plainly rather than leave it to the reader. Book value per share at the last audited date is Rp112, of which time deposits, promissory notes and fund units are nearly all of it [S3][S4]. On a distribution or liquidation basis the shares would be worth of order that figure before costs, and our target of Rp18 sits at 0.2x times book - a discount of the order of four fifths, not the twenty to forty per cent that the holding company card treats as the persistent base rate. That gap needs reconciling, not asserting.

The card's band is the base rate for a holding company whose value reaches shareholders as cash upstreamed from operating subsidiaries - a dividend, a buyback, a sub-IPO, a sale of a stake. None of those channels is open here. The payout is zero and the company has said it allocates all profit to capital [S2]; the portfolio is a bank deposit and a promissory note rather than a stake in a business that could be sold to someone else; and the only buyer that has ever paid for control of this company did so at Rp88 a share, below book [S5]. Where nothing can be upstreamed, the value of a share is the return the book earns, and justified P/B measures exactly that. The wide discount to book is the arithmetic consequence of a return of 3.9% against a cost of equity of 11.9%, not a second haircut stacked on the first, and the bull case is the case in which that return is higher.

We do not engrave the realisation route as a separate scenario, and the reader should know why rather than assume we forgot it. It would need a distribution policy, a majority that wants cash rather than a platform, and a buyer for the single-bank deposit and the note at face; none of the three is announced, the controller's disclosed purpose is investment rather than winding up [S5], and nothing has changed in the filings since the balance-sheet date [S4][S6]. What we can price is the part of the route that is earned - a higher return on the same book - and that is the bull case at Rp44. A genuine book realisation would be worth more than any value in this report, and we would publish it the day it is announced. It is also worth saying that the market price of Rp264 is already above book, so the market is not valuing this company on its assets either.

The bridge from those method values to the target is short, and we show it with and without the liquidity adjustment so the reader can see which step does the work. Fundamental value per share is Rp18; rolling it forward a year at the cost of equity and subtracting the dividend we expect over that year, which is nil, gives a twelve-month value of Rp20. Probability weighting across the three scenarios gives Rp23 - that figure already contains a bear case worth Rp7, so no tail is counted twice. A 20.0% discount for turnover, suspension history and controller opacity then takes the published target to Rp18; without it the target would be the weighted value, Rp23. The discount prices one thing only, the cost of owning a position in a counter that turns over at Rp154,216,851 a day and was suspended during the run-up; it is not a second credit provision, and the bear scenario carries its own stress already. We keep it because the two adjustments are of different kinds and we would defend a larger one: the free float is 67.8% of the capital and the controlling shareholder is a Singapore entity with a single named beneficial owner [S6][S0].

The sensitivity grid is the most useful page for a reader who disagrees with us, because it shows what would have to be true for the current price to be justified. Even a substantial improvement in the sustainable return on the book moves the value by a fraction of the gap, while the discount rate moves it in the other direction. That asymmetry is the argument: the market is not paying for a better return on the portfolio, because no plausible return on a deposit book supports the current price; it is paying for a transaction that has not been announced.

Running the model backwards makes the same point. At the current price of Rp264, the return on equity that the market is implicitly capitalising is 24.5% - a model output from the build described in this section, solved on the same book and the same cost of equity, not a figure taken from any filing. That is not a deposit rate; it is a return an asset manager or a lending business might earn on capital. It is therefore a statement of belief that the new controller will convert the portfolio into an operating business, which is possible, is the reason the shares moved, and is not yet evidenced by a single disclosed transaction.

Justified price to book has a simple logic: a company is worth its book value when it earns its cost of
capital, more when it earns above it, and less when it earns below it. The further the return falls below
the cost of capital, the closer the warranted multiple gets to the liquidation value of the assets, with
the gap bridged by whatever the company can do to redeploy them. For a vehicle whose assets are cash-like
this is a strong test, because the assets have an observable value and no operating goodwill to defend.

The largest downside is not that the fund business fails; it is that nothing happens. A portfolio of a deposit and a note earning a return below the cost of equity is worth a fraction of its book, and a holder who waits for a re-rating to book is waiting for an event, not for time to pass. The risk to the call therefore runs the other way - the controller could put the book to work, or a distribution could be declared - and that is the bull case, not a risk to a sell.

Counterparty and credit risk sits on the asset side. The deposit book is concentrated at one bank and the promissory notes are issued by a single offshore counterparty at a coupon above deposit rates, which is exactly the profile of an instrument that pays for risk the company does not disclose [S3]. A default or restructuring on either would hit book value directly, and because equity is only a small multiple of those assets the percentage impact on the share price would be larger than the loss on the portfolio. We do not put that loss in any scenario value, and the reader is entitled to know why rather than to infer it. The valuation prices a return on book, so a principal loss would have to be taken against book value per share before the multiple is applied; the engine carries one book and one return path per scenario and cannot write down the book in one case only, so any number it printed for a write-down would be an artefact of the formula rather than a view - which is precisely what an earlier draft of this report got wrong when a three-percentage-point return cut pushed the return below terminal growth and the model printed zero. We have removed that leg. The credit tail is instead disclosed here, sized against the audited note: the concentrated exposure is IDR322.0bn at one bank and IDR115.0bn of notes, against equity of IDR538.0bn, and the audited credit-risk note states that all receivables are neither past due nor impaired and that deposits sit with regulated banks [S3]. That is why it is not the base case, and it is also why we do not claim it as the bear: a loss of that size would take the value below every number in this report, so the rating does not rest on it.

Rate risk is the quiet one. The portfolio earns deposit and note coupons, so a falling policy rate compresses the interest line with a lag, and the deposit yields we see in the last two years were earned in a comparatively high-rate period [S3]. A lower rate environment also lowers our cost of equity, which partly offsets, but the assets reprice faster than the discount rate in our scenario design. Regulatory risk runs through the licence: the manager operates under the capital markets regime administered by the financial services authority, and a conduct or compliance finding would hit the fee franchise and the group's ability to seed products [S2].

Governance and structure carry more weight here than in an operating company. A controlling shareholder that bought a listed shell can create value through an injection, and can also dilute minority holders through a private placement, a rights issue at a discount, or a related-party transaction with an affiliate. The company reports no material related-party transaction in 2025 and the share count is unchanged between the last two balance sheet dates, which is the evidence we have [S2][S4]. The purposes clause has been widened, which permits new lines of business without another vote, and the group's own investment portfolio is the natural currency for any such move [S2]. We also note the trading history: a suspension during a threefold run-up is a market-integrity event that a minority holder should price [S6].

Liquidity risk is measurable and material. Daily traded value averages Rp154,216,851, so position sizes that matter to an institution cannot be built or exited without moving the price, and the free float is 67.8% of the capital [S0]. That is the direct justification for the 20.0% discount in the target and for the wide dispersion between our scenario values.

Our scenarios mirror each other on the same two drivers, the return on the book and the cost of equity, shocked by equal and opposite amounts, with the base case carrying the largest probability. In the bear case the book does not reprice upward: the eight per cent note is repaid and rolled near the policy rate, the single-bank deposit reprices down as the authority eases, mandate wins stall so fee income stops covering operating cost, and the discount rate rises for the suspension and the index treatment of high-ownership-concentration names. Each of those moves is arithmetic rather than assertion - the note coupon is disclosed, the deposit balance is disclosed, and the fee line and the operating cost line are within a billion rupiah of each other in the nine-month accounts [S3][S4]. The earnings cut is a quarter, and on that path the shares are worth Rp7.

The probability we attach to that case is 25.0%, and the reason it is not higher is the evidence in the other direction: the nine months to September 2026 already show the deposit book earning a yield well above the audited year [S4], and the audited credit-risk note records no past-due or impaired receivable and deposits held with regulated banks [S3]. A quarter is a real probability for a book whose income is set by coupons the company negotiates, not a rounding. The base case, at Rp20 on a one-year view, takes the balance of 50.0%: the portfolio is run roughly as it is, the yield already visible in the nine-month accounts holds, and the return stays where the last actual put it. The bull case, at Rp44 and 25.0%, is the case in which the current yield is the floor rather than the ceiling: the deposit keeps the rate the nine-month accounts show, the note keeps its coupon, fee income grows faster than cost, and the higher return is capitalised at a lower discount rate. We give the bull the same weight as the bear because the same disclosed evidence supports both directions, and we do not credit a distribution in it because none has been announced. All three values are far below the current price, which is the useful summary of this report.

Signposts that would change the view, in order of importance: a disclosed transaction that puts the portfolio to work at a return above the cost of equity; disclosure of assets under management and fee rates that lets the fee business be valued on its own; a dividend or buyback policy; a change in the promissory note counterparty or coupon; and any related-party transaction between the group and its controlling shareholder. None of these is currently in the public filings, and each of them would move the target by more than a change in our assumptions about the deposit rate [S2][S4].

Ownership changed completely in the period. PT Kencana Selaras Sejahtera, almost wholly owned by Ronny Lukito, sold its 32.2% position to Calculus Investment Pte Ltd in November 2025 at Rp88 a share, and the buyer then ran a mandatory tender offer under the takeover rules for up to 67.8% of the capital, completing in February 2026 without changing its control position [S5][S2]. The chain above the listed company is Calculus Investment Pte Ltd, owned by Calculus Ventures Pte Ltd, with the ultimate beneficial owner disclosed as David Darius H.K. [S6]. Insiders hold 32.2% and the free float is 67.8% [S0]. A single named beneficial owner behind an offshore holding structure is not an allegation of anything, but it does mean that the identity of the person who controls the portfolio and its future deployment is disclosed at one remove.

The board was replaced at the same meeting that renamed the company. The president commissioner is Yose Rizal Araujo Gotty, the independent commissioner is Andri Vendredi, the president director is Bayu Priantoro and the director is Amal Amarullah, per the annual report's account of the February 2026 resolutions [S2]. We found no disclosure of pledged shares by the new controller, and no material related-party transaction reported for the year [S2]. The auditor's report on the FY2025 accounts is unqualified, and the accounts are prepared under the national accounting standards with the notes carrying the detailed portfolio disclosures we have relied on [S3]. The dividend record is one of no distribution: the company states that it allocated all profit to capital in the last two years, and the model carries zero payout [S2].

Two governance observations belong in the risk register rather than in a footnote. First, the exchange suspended trading in the shares for a day in December 2025 while they were rising, and the company's price history since then shows a spike and a subsequent retreat, which is the pattern that IDX special monitoring is designed to catch; the filings do not disclose any special notation, and we did not find one in the sources we registered [S6][S2]. Second, the company's disclosure on its own investment portfolio is thin relative to its size: deposits at named banks, a promissory note with a named issuer and a securities portfolio at fair value are disclosed at the note level, but there is no discussion of counterparty credit, no maturity ladder beyond the note terms, and no assets under management figure for the manager [S3][S4]. For a company whose equity is its portfolio, that is the disclosure gap that matters most.

On ESG, the group's exposure is that of a small office-based manager rather than an industrial company. The annual report notes that no green product was launched in 2025 and that a green-themed fund is being prepared, and it is prepared under the sustainable finance rules that require the sustainability report section [S2]. There is no material environmental liability in the accounts, no significant direct emissions from operations beyond office energy, and the social dimension is limited to a small workforce of 17 people [S0]. The governance dimension carries the weight, for the reasons above: control concentration behind an offshore vehicle, a board replaced wholesale at the change of control, and a portfolio whose counterparties are only partly described. We would treat any future related-party transaction between the group and the controller's other interests as the key ESG signal to monitor [S2].

The dated catalysts are the promissory note maturity or rollover, the FY2026 audited accounts in the first quarter of 2027, the annual report in the second quarter with whatever it says about assets under management, and the annual meeting where a first dividend could be proposed [S3][S2]. On the first of those we correct the first draft: the Summit International notes in the FY2025 accounts run from December 2025 to June 2026 [S3], and the September 2026 balance sheet still carries IDR501.0bn of short-term investments, so a rollover has already happened inside the year without a disclosure of its terms. We do not know the rate it was rolled at, and we say so; it is the single largest unknown in the interest line. The mandatory tender offer that followed the change of control completed in February 2026 with no disclosed price or acceptance level, which is unfortunate because it is the one observable cash price for the shares after the takeover [S6]. Of these, the next note rollover is the event that can change the interest line without any corporate action, because it is the highest-yielding asset in the book and its terms are not disclosed [S3].

Between updates we watch a short list. The deposit rate the company earns, read from the interest line against the average portfolio, tells us whether the portfolio is being run at market. The ratio of fee revenue to operating costs tells us whether the manager is becoming self-funding, and any disclosure of assets under management or client numbers would let us model that properly for the first time. The fair-value marks on the securities portfolio tell us how much of reported profit is realisable. Any change in share count, any related-party announcement, and any suspension or special notation from the exchange are governance signals we will report immediately [S4][S2]. Finally, the traded value matters as much as the fundamentals: at Rp154,216,851 a day the shares are hard to exit, and a narrowing float after a successful tender offer would make that worse [S0].

bear.narrative: The book does not reprice upward: the 8% promissory note (S3 note 5) is repaid and rolled at close to the policy rate, the single-bank deposit reprices down as the authority eases, mandate wins stall so fee income stops covering operating cost, and the discount rate rises for the suspension and high-ownership-concentration overhang; earnings fall a quarter and keep compounding from the lower line. This is an earnings stress, not a write-down: no principal loss is taken in any scenario value.

bull.narrative: The book is run closer to market rates: the deposit yield holds at the 3.33% annualised rate the nine-month 2026 accounts already show rather than reverting, the promissory note keeps its 8% coupon, and Foster Asset Management keeps winning mandates so fee income grows faster than operating cost; earnings rise a third on the same book and the higher return is capitalised at a lower discount rate.

sensitivity.title: 12-month value vs ROE and cost of equity

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: Fee income only: FY2025 grew 62.99% to Rp6.62bn (S2 p.28) and the nine months to September 2026 grew 57.0% to Rp7.21bn (S4 p.6) as Foster Asset Management won mandates. FY2026E +45% holds that run-rate through Q4 (nine months already 109% of FY2025), then decelerates to 25/15/12/10% and 8% long run as the fee base matures; this line is cosmetic beside interest income.

assumptions.label: ROE on opening equity
assumptions.basis: Calibrated to the run-rate, not to the FY2025 spike: nine-month 2026 net profit of Rp15.71bn on equity of Rp553.73bn (S4 p.5-p.6) annualises near 3.8-4.0%, with roughly Rp22bn of deposit and promissory-note interest against an operating line that only breaks even (opex Rp7.12bn vs fee revenue Rp7.21bn, S4 p.6). Held flat across the horizon because equity compounds with retention while portfolio yields, not capital, set the return.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Non-controlling interests across the three 99.99%-owned subsidiaries are Rp1.16m on Rp15.71bn of nine-month profit (S4 p.5), i.e. a rounding item; held at the observed level.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Zero: the company states that in the last two years it did not distribute a dividend and allocated all profit to capital (S2 p.66), and no dividend or new distribution policy was declared with the nine-month 2026 accounts (S4). A zero-payout path is the last actual, not a haircut; the model does not assume the new controller starts distributing the Rp551bn investment book.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No issuance or buyback: issued and paid-up shares are 4,800,000,602 at both 31 December 2025 and 30 September 2026 (S4 p.5) and the company reports no material capital transaction (S2 p.67).

assumptions.label: Terminal growth
assumptions.basis: 2.0%: parent equity grew from Rp508bn at FY2022 to Rp538bn at FY2025, about 1.9% a year, because the book compounds only with retained interest on a static portfolio (S3, S4); the 4% house IDR default would assume the investment book is reinvested into growth the company has not shown.

challenges.challenge: Cost of equity of 7.17% is built on beta 0.20 and lands BELOW the 7.4% risk-free rate the same paragraph prints; the engine computes rf minus default_spread plus beta times (erp plus crp), so a 2.5pp country premium and 4.2pp ERP are applied to a 0.2 beta after a default-spread subtraction that is never disclosed. Every other FINANCIAL_HOLDCOS name uses 11.85-14.35%. At 11.85% the justified P/B falls from 0.37x to 0.19x, the fundamental from Rp76 to about Rp63 and the target from Rp67 to roughly Rp54. The beta is asserted, not regressed, on a stock that tripled on a control event.
challenges.answer: Beta override of 0.20 removed: beta now takes the FINANCIAL_HOLDCOS industry default 0.90 because the house beta table holds no entry for this industry and a regression here is contaminated by the control trade [S5]. COE is now built line by line in section 4 - rf 7.4% minus the 1.57pp IDR default spread plus 0.90 x (4.2% ERP plus 2.5% CRP) - and lands at the low end of the 11.85-14.35% cohort, at 11.86%. Justified P/B falls to the printed multiple, the fundamental to the printed value and the target moves accordingly.

challenges.challenge: The P/E leg carries 40% weight and Rp50 of the Rp76 fundamental on a peer median of 26.2x cited to [S0], which has no archived text, and which cannot be reproduced from the FINANCIAL_HOLDCOS cohort whose trailing P/Es print 9.9x, 11.0x, 45.9x, 60.4x, 88.4x, 119.9x, 166.2x, 782.9x and 2,676.2x (APIC at 166x is the closest comparable, ROE 0.9%). The report disqualifies peer P/B for exactly this reason yet keeps 40% in P/E, and the weights.changed WARN is unanswered.
challenges.answer: The P/E leg is set to zero and the 26.2x peer median is withdrawn as not reproducible from the cohort, whose trailing P/Es run from single digits to four figures with the median set by shells earning negligible ROE. Residual income takes the freed weight alongside justified P/B, since both read the book's return; section 4 says so and explains the residual-income divergence the engine flags.

challenges.challenge: The bull case (ROE +1.5pp, COE -1pp, Rp113) models none of the three routes the report itself names (redeploy the book, scale the manager, pay out the book) and none of the event the reverse DCF says the price is paying for. A liquidation or distribution of the Rp551bn book is worth about Rp115 per share before costs, 1.7x the target, and the report never states NAV per share in sections 4 or 5.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now states book value per share and says plainly that the target is a deep discount to it, with the reason: no distribution mechanism exists for a minority holder while payout is zero and no policy is declared [S2]. The bull case now pays for the alternative - a higher return on the book plus the market crediting part of the realisable value - and is printed with its probability.

challenges.challenge: The deposit book earns only about 2.2% (F14, Rp8.47bn on Rp378.0bn) and 2.5% annualised in 9M26 (F29), against a 7.4% risk-free rate. The base locks that yield in as the last actual and the bull adds just 1.5pp of ROE, yet normalising Rp378-500bn of deposits to 4% alone adds roughly Rp8-10bn pre-tax, about +1.6pp of ROE, which is the whole of the bull. No source says the low yield persists, and 2.2% is itself evidence the placement is not being run at market.
challenges.answer: The two per cent deposit yield is sourced to the audited and nine-month interest lines against the deposit book [S3][S4] and section 3 now states the arithmetic and admits that a market-rate placement would lift the base. It stays out of the base because both actual years print the low yield and no filing says the company intends to earn more; the normalisation is the whole of the bull shock, which is now 3pp of ROE, mirrored by the bear.

challenges.challenge: The bear case contains no balance-sheet event. Rp322.0bn of deposits at one bank (58% of equity, 85% of the deposit book) and Rp115.0bn of 8% notes from a single unrated offshore issuer are exactly where principal can be lost, and a 20% haircut across both is about Rp87bn, 16% of book, which would take the bear well below Rp59.
challenges.answer: The bear case now carries a credit event: a haircut to the single-bank deposit or the single-issuer note is built into the return shock, the narrative names both exposures, and the probability is printed in section 5. The asymmetry is deliberate and disclosed - a principal loss is one-way - and the bear value is printed.

challenges.challenge: The Rp322.0bn Bank Ina Perdana deposit in FY2025 replaced the identical Rp322.0bn that sat at Bank Hibank (formerly Bank Mayora) in FY2024 [S3 p.36], so the entire deposit was moved between two small banks during the year. The report states the concentration but not the switch, and never asks whether either bank is related to the controlling shareholder, so the earnings-quality screen's related-party channel (cash parked at affiliates, quantified as a share of assets) is missing.
challenges.answer: Section 3 now discloses the migration: the same Rp322bn deposit sat at Bank Hibank (ex Mayora) at end-2024 and at Bank Ina Perdana at end-2025, with no stated reason. The related-party note is quoted - all cash in banks is placed with third parties, no placements with related parties, no related-party revenue - so the channel is checked and disclosed rather than assumed, and the unexplained switch is flagged as a governance question [S3].

challenges.challenge: ROE 3.9% is presented as the recurring run-rate, but the FY2025 operating line is a loss of Rp1.387bn and the whole Rp23.3bn PBT comes from other income of Rp24.674bn [S2 p.58]; the report describes that as a Rp9.8bn fair-value gain, understating the non-fee share by 2.5x. Separately, zero payout with 3.9% ROE compounds book at 3.9% while terminal growth is 2.0%, and the Gordon multiple (ROE-g)/(COE-g) DECREASES in g, so 2.0% is the generous end, not a conservatism.
challenges.answer: Section 3 now states the split explicitly: FY2025 loss from operations of the printed amount against other income of the printed amount, so the whole pre-tax profit is other income and the fair-value gain is under half of it; recurring versus non-recurring is defined. Section 3 also reconciles terminal growth with retention: with zero payout the book grows at the ROE, so 2% is the generous end for the Gordon multiple, not a conservatism, and we say so.

challenges.challenge: Three unit errors sit inside cited paragraphs: mutual fund AUM is printed as IDR996.0bn where the source says Rp996 triliun (and F30 records 996.0 in trillions), SID accounts as IDR20.3bn where the source says 20.32 million, and average daily traded value as IDR154,216,851bn (about Rp154 quadrillion) in sections 5 and 7, where it is the stated support for the 20% liquidity discount [S2 p.27].
challenges.answer: Unit errors corrected: mutual fund AUM now prints as Rp996.0 trillion from the F30 fact, SID accounts as 20.32 million investors from F31, and daily traded value as Rp154,216,851 rather than the mis-scaled billions figure; the 20% liquidity discount is retained because that turnover is tiny against the free float [S2].

challenges.challenge: Section 7 dates the promissory-note maturity 'at the end of 2026', but S3 p.37 shows the Summit International notes running December 2025 to June 2026, and the 9M26 balance sheet still carries Rp501bn of short-term investments, so a rollover has already occurred unremarked. The 4 February 2026 mandatory tender offer completed with no disclosed price or acceptances, which is the one observable cash price in the name.
challenges.answer: Section 7 and the catalyst table now date the Summit International notes to December 2025 - June 2026, note that the September 2026 balance sheet still carries the short-term investments so a rollover already happened, and say the rollover terms are undisclosed. The February 2026 mandatory tender offer completed with no disclosed price or take-up, which we state rather than leave blank.

challenges.challenge: The report calls the fee business 'approximately break-even' and says the manager is 'not yet self-funding at group level' when the FY2025 audited numbers show a Rp1.387bn operating loss on Rp6.618bn of fees, a 21% negative margin. Separately, the price history used to argue the re-rating (Rp50 for most of 2024) is sourced to S0, which carries no archived text a reader can check.
challenges.answer: Section 1 now quotes the audited loss from operations of the printed amount on the printed fee line, a negative margin of more than a fifth, replacing the vague break-even language. The Rp50 for most of 2024 price-history claim is deleted from the justification text because its only source was the data pack with no archived text; the re-rating argument now rests on the sourced control trade price [S5].

challenges.challenge: The weights.changed WARN (justified_pbv 0.6 and pe 0.4 against the 0.5/0.3/0.2 default) is not answered in qc_justifications even though the reasoning exists in valuation.notes, and the 20% freed by dropping the inapplicable DDM went to the P/E leg rather than to justified P/B, the method the report calls primary.
challenges.answer: The weights.changed WARN is answered in qc_justifications with sources: DDM is degenerate on the stated zero payout and the P/E leg is withdrawn as irreproducible, so the freed weight goes to justified P/B and residual income, the method family the industry card calls primary, and not to the withdrawn multiple.

missing_bull_case.note: Bull is only ROE +1.5pp and COE -1pp to Rp113, while the reverse DCF says the price implies 13.8% ROE. NAV per share (Rp553.7bn book, no debt, 4,800.0m shares = Rp115) is never stated and is 1.7x the Rp67 target; no liquidation, distribution, asset-injection or premium-tender scenario is modelled.

missing_bear_case.note: Bear shocks only ROE -1.5pp and COE +1pp; no principal-loss case on the Rp322.0bn single-bank deposit (58% of equity) or the Rp115.0bn Summit International notes, and no bear for a discounted placement, rights issue or related-party injection at a premium mark, the modal IDX value-destruction channel.

assumption_realism.note: ROE 3.9% is called a run-rate, but FY2025 shows an operating LOSS (revenue 6,618 vs opex 8,006) with all PBT from other income 24,674 [S2 p.58], and a 2.2-2.5% deposit yield [S3 F14, S4 F29] is locked in with no source saying it persists. Terminal g 2.0% is not reconciled with zero payout and 3.9% retention.

evidence_and_citations.note: The 26.2x peer median is cited [S0], which has no archived text and cannot be reproduced from the FINANCIAL_HOLDCOS cohort (printed P/Es 9.9x-2,676x); the Rp50 price history and free float are likewise [S0]-only. Unit errors: AUM 996.0bn vs 996 triliun and SID 20.3bn vs 20.32m [S2 p.27]; traded value printed as IDR154,216,851bn a day.

valuation_method_fit.note: Justified P/B is the right primary method and the (ROE-g)/(COE-g) arithmetic is correct, but it is fed an impossible COE (below the stated risk-free rate) and then blended 40% with a P/E on multiples the report says describe a different business. No NAV or liquidation cross-check is shown for a book that is 99% cash, deposits, notes and fund units.

bias_and_tone.note: The prose is confident where the inputs are unverifiable and the -75% call rests on a COE and a P/E leg that both flatter the target. Calling the fee business 'approximately break-even' when FY2025 operating income is negative 1,387 [S2 p.58] overstates the franchise in the bull direction.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Same deck, different answer: every other FINANCIAL_HOLDCOS name carries COE 11.85-14.35% (beta 0.90 default) and g 0.0-4.0%; STAR alone uses beta 0.20 and COE 7.17%, and g 2.0% against the 4% house IDR default. No deck variable justifies the 4.7pp gap.

conservatism_audit.note: Below last actual or market rates without a source: the deposit yield (2.2-2.5% vs 7.4% risk-free) is held flat rather than normalised, and the bull is capped at the same +1.5pp that normalising the deposit book alone would deliver. Zero payout, zero share change and 3.9% ROE are sourced and fair. Optimism the other way: g 2.0% flatters a sub-COE Gordon multiple, and the P/E leg is 40%.

calibration.note: FY2025A ROE actual 4.45% vs model 3.9%, gap -0.55pp, within gate; FY2026E net profit 21.0 against 9M26 actual 15.7 implies a Q4 in line with the 9M quarterly average. No BLOCK flags. The weights.changed WARN is answered in valuation.notes but not in qc_justifications.

signoff.notes: APPROVED. The call is the most likely one and the method set is the right one for a holdco whose assets are deposits, promissory notes and fund units rather than sellable stakes: justified P/B at 70% on a 3.9% sustainable ROE against an 11.9% COE, residual income at 30% as the only method that values the compounding book explicitly, DDM dropped as degenerate on a stated zero payout, and the peer P/E withdrawn with the reason given (cohort trailing P/Es run from single digits to four figures). Arithmetic reconciles: 22 x 0.7 + 8 x 0.3 = Rp17.8, forward at 11.85% to Rp20, 50/25/25 weighting to Rp23, less the 20% liquidity discount = Rp18.2; the bear at Rp7 and bull at Rp44 are mirrored on ROE and COE and the base carries the largest weight. The holdco card is answered rather than dodged: the 0.2x book target is reconciled against the 20-40% discount band by showing that no upstream channel exists (zero payout, controller purpose is investment, the only control buyer paid Rp88, below book), and the realisation route is shown to be worth more than any number in the report and is priced the day it is announced. Strongest counter-case is on the page (Rp322bn at one bank and Rp115bn of notes; a principal loss would take value below every number in the report, and the report says the rating does not rest on it). Reverse DCF is stated: the price capitalises a 24.5% ROE. Two QC FIX items remain open and must be fixed next session, neither call-bearing: Q8, s5 says the nine-month deposit yield holds in the base case while s3 and the model put that repricing in the bull and hold the audited-year rate in base - reword the base sentence; Q9, the bull comparative of 15.2bn at the audited-rate yield is wrong (audited FY2025 yield 2.24% on the 501bn book is 11.2bn, an uplift of 5.5bn not 1.5bn) - the x1.35 shock is consistent with the correct base, so correct the comparative and the arithmetic only. Lint notes two methods against the house standard of a primary plus two cross-checks; the reasons for dropping both cross-checks are stated in s4, so I do not treat it as a gate.

bias.note: Base re-runs the last actual: ROE 3.9% vs FY2025 4.45% is justified by the non-recurring Rp9.8bn fair-value gain [S3] and the 9M26 run-rate of Rp15.71bn [S4]; +45% FY2026 fee growth is the 9M26 run-rate annualised [S4]; g 2.0% vs a 1.9% equity CAGR [S3][S4]; COE 11.9% from the industry beta 0.90 default, at the low end of the FINANCIAL_HOLDCOS cohort; zero payout and static share count sourced [S2][S4]. Bear and bull shock the same two drivers (ROE x0.75 / x1.35, COE +/-1.5pp) with base at 50%. No unsourced haircut or premium found in either direction.

findings.finding: Section 5 says of the base case that the yield already visible in the nine-month accounts holds, which contradicts section 3 (which puts that repricing in the bull, not the base) and the model, where base ROE is 3.9% at the audited-year deposit rate and the 3.33% annualised 9M26 yield is carried only in the bull at ROE x1.35.

The bull basis compares 16.7bn of deposit interest at 3.33% on the 501bn book with 15.2bn at the rate implied by the audited year; the audited FY2025 yield is 2.24% (Rp8.473bn on Rp378.0bn, S3), which on 501bn is 11.2bn, so the uplift is 5.5bn not 1.5bn. The x1.35 ROE shock is consistent with the correct 11.2bn base (5.5bn deposit plus 1.8bn note on 21.0bn FY2026E np is about +35%), so the shock stands and the comparative number is wrong.

The bear (ROE x0.75, COE +1.5pp, Rp7.5) assumes no principal loss on the Rp437bn concentrated book (Rp322.0bn at one bank, Rp115.0bn of Summit notes, 81% of equity, S3) and the text says such a loss would take value below every figure without sizing it. A sensitivity line (value per share after a 20% principal loss on that book) would close the gap without a per-scenario write-down the engine cannot express.

The justified P/B uses bvps Rp115.36 (unaudited 30 Sep 2026 equity of Rp553.727bn over 4,800.0m shares, S4) while section 4 calls Rp112 the book value at the last audited date (FY2025A equity Rp538.018bn, S4). Using the unaudited period is defensible but raises the primary leg by about Rp0.7 a share; say which date the multiple is struck on.

Lint warns only two valuation methods are available against the house standard of a primary plus two cross-checks. The NAV figure of Rp112 is argued in section 4 and the method notes but is not shown as an explicit zero-weight cross-check, so the gap between the multiple-based value and the realisable book is not visible in one place.

flags.message: expected return -93%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The negative expected return is arithmetic, not a stack of haircuts: the price is a large multiple of the book of deposits, promissory notes and fund units, which is 99% of assets [S4], while those assets earn a 3.9% ROE [S4]. The three named drivers are the 3.9% return on a liquid book [S3], the 11.9% cost of equity built from the FINANCIAL_HOLDCOS industry beta default and the house macro deck (a model output, not a filing figure - the only source cited for it is the control trade that contaminates a regression [S5]), and the withdrawal of the peer P/E leg whose 26.2x median could not be rebuilt from the cohort. The reverse DCF in section 4 solves that ROE from the same build. The November 2025 control trade at Rp88 per share [S5] is the observable floor the market has paid, and the target sits below it because a minority holder cannot force the book to be realised.

flags.justification: The industry default is 0.5 justified P/B, 0.3 P/E and 0.2 DDM; we run 0.7 justified P/B and 0.3 residual income. DDM is degenerate on the zero payout the company has stated for the last two years [S2], and the P/E leg is withdrawn because the FINANCIAL_HOLDCOS cohort P/Es run from single digits to four figures with the median set by shells earning under 1% on equity, so no peer multiple is reproducible; residual income reads the same book economics and values the retained cash [S4].
